motion: For the last four years, America got the Middle East right.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Can you identify a safer alternative than setting limits, supporting partners, and avoiding another costly regional war? If your plan requires open-ended commitments, why should Americans trust it?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: A partner that delays protecting its communities because American backing seems doubtful can suffer avoidable harm before any response arrives. That human cost shows why an unclear regional policy was wrong.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. The motion is: for the last four years, America got the Middle East right. Betsy supports it, and Nina opposes it. Each has thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire and thirty-second closings. I will give a ten-second cue.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: America pursued steadier partnerships, contained wider conflict, and kept pressure on violent groups without pretending every dispute has a quick fix. Getting it right means protecting interests while leaving room for regional responsibility. That is what this approach did. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You can come in, Nina.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Calling restraint success ignores people left exposed when promises became uncertain. A policy can avoid a larger fight and still fail.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But your standard makes any unresolved danger-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Can you let her speak please?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: -because uncertain backing invites rivals to test every boundary. Partners need clear commitments, not careful phrases that can be read as retreat.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, Nina.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Over four years, that uncertainty weakened deterrence, so America did not get the region right. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. Now onto round two. And round two is where the debaters address one another directly. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If this policy got the region right, why did partners repeatedly have to wonder whether support would arrive when threats rose? How does uncertainty create deterrence rather than invite testing?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Consider a partner facing attacks from armed groups: instead of sending Americans into another open-ended ground fight, America supplied support and demanded local responsibility. That protects people without deepening war, proving the approach was right.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That example raises the separate question of who carries the moral burden after a conflict ends, especially families whose homes and routines have already been broken. Debates over apologies and memory can shape whether those families trust any outside promise.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: What we are talking about here is for the last four years, America got the Middle East right. We're not going back into history.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The question is whether America got the Middle East right over these four years, and leaving partners unsure during danger was the wrong course. Prudence without dependable commitment is not sound policy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your point is that partners felt unsure, but you treat certainty as if it requires automatic military action. Clear limits can be more credible than broad promises America cannot responsibly keep.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree that America should not promise every partner unlimited help. But the main failure was mixed signals at crucial moments, and that made both friends and adversaries doubt American resolve.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If your answer is stronger commitments, where do you draw the line before America is dragged into every local dispute? You cannot call restraint failure while refusing to say what conflict you would-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I reject the premise that dependable support means entering every dispute. Decisions about equipment and training matter too, but the motion concerns the overall record, and that record made deterrence less believable.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The weakest part of that claim is calling the record less believable without showing why measured support is weakness. America retained leverage, avoided reckless escalation, and made partners carry more of their own defense.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I would not send America into every conflict; that is not my position. Your claim that leverage remained misses the point: leverage means little when opponents believe hesitation will prevent a firm response.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your point is that hesitation invited challenges, but you equate a deliberate choice with paralysis. A firm response can be targeted, limited, and credible without turning every challenge into a wider war.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left, both of you.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I accept that targeted action can sometimes prevent a wider war. Yet the broader pattern lacked a dependable-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time's up. We need to move into our closing round. Betsy, you are up first with that, as you were at the beginning.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The opposition calls limits uncertainty, but limitless promises are less believable and more dangerous. America supported partners, checked violent threats, and avoided being pulled into another sprawling war. That combination of restraint and resolve got the Middle East right. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Nina wants to answer that.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: My strongest point is simple: deterrence depends on dependable commitments, and the last four years sent mixed signals when they mattered most. Avoiding a larger war can be wise, but it is not enough if partners and opponents both question whether America will act. A sound policy must make the answer clear.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds left.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: It did not, and that uncertainty made the regional approach wrong. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Betsy and Nina, for a vigorous debate. That concludes our discussion of the motion.
